# Determinants of Artificial Intelligence Addiction: Anxiety, Self-Efficacy, Attitudes, Literacy, Perceived Ease of Use, Behavioral Intention, and Perceived Usefulness

Merve Canbeldek Erol[a](#determinants-of-artificial-intelligence-addiction-anxiety-self-efficacy-attitudes-literacy-perceived-ease-of-use-behavioral-intention-and-perceived-usefulness) [,](http://orcid.org/0000-0003-3100-2220) Ahmet Erol[a](#determinants-of-artificial-intelligence-addiction-anxiety-self-efficacy-attitudes-literacy-perceived-ease-of-use-behavioral-intention-and-perceived-usefulness) [,](http://orcid.org/0000-0002-7538-952X) Mustafa Erol[b](#determinants-of-artificial-intelligence-addiction-anxiety-self-efficacy-attitudes-literacy-perceived-ease-of-use-behavioral-intention-and-perceived-usefulness) and Kadriye Selin Budak Topaloglu[c](#determinants-of-artificial-intelligence-addiction-anxiety-self-efficacy-attitudes-literacy-perceived-ease-of-use-behavioral-intention-and-perceived-usefulness)

aDepartment of Preschool Education Program, Pamukkale University, Denizli, T€urkiye; bDepartment of Primary Education Program, Yıldız Technical University, \_Istanbul, Turkiye;€ cChild Care and Youth Services Department, Bilecik S¸eyh Edebali University, Bilecik, T€urkiye

## ABSTRACT KEYWORDS This study examined the direct and indirect effects of early childhood educators’ and can- AI addiction; AI literacy; didates’ (ECE-C) AI self-efficacy, anxiety, literacy, positive and negative attitudes, perceived AI self-efficacy; AI anxiety; ease of use, perceived usefulness, and behavioral intention on their addiction to artificial AI attitudes intelligence (AI). Data were collected using the Teachers’ Acceptance of AI Instrument (TAAI),

the Dependence on Artificial Intelligence Scale (DAIS), the General Attitudes toward Artificial Intelligence Scale (GAAIS), and the Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale (AILS). The results

revealed that the strongest predictor of AI addiction was a positive attitude toward AI, whereas a negative attitude and anxiety increased addiction. In contrast, self-efficacy

emerged as a protective factor that reduced addiction. AI self-efficacy was positively pre- dicted by perceived ease of use, behavioral intention, AI literacy, and, to a lesser extent,

perceived usefulness. While AI literacy indirectly reduced addiction via self-efficacy, it also showed an enhancing effect on addiction through anxiety.

1. Introduction Rapid advances in digital technologies have fundamentally transformed human life, influencing how individuals think, learn, communicate, and work. Among these transformative innovations, artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as one of the most significant developments of the 21st century, drawing increasing attention from researchers, educators, and policymakers worldwide. In today’s world, emerg- ing technologies are reshaping nearly all aspects of life, including work, entertainment, social relation- ships, and learning (Shanmugasundaram & Tamilarasu, 2023). One of the most influential technologies is AI (Breckner et al., 2025; Wei et al., 2025). The development and integration of AI into society have begun to transform the ways we learn, interact, and work (Pasch & Ha, 2025; Qian et al., 2024;

<div></div>

1. Wang et al., 2024). As a result of this transformation, it is argued that every individual who actively participates in society must acquire the ability to engage effectively with AI applications (Ng et al., 2021a), to cultivate proactive citizens (Kong et al., 2022). In this regard, particular emphasis has been placed on the need to enhance teachers’ AI-related digital competencies in alignment with the trans- formation of 21st-century skills (Liebenow et al., 2025; Ng et al., 2023).

Technology-enhanced learning environments, when combined with effective pedagogical practices, have great potential to increase students’ engagement in learning, thereby supporting their academic per- formance and promoting the development of higher-order skills (S. Wang et al., 2024; Xu, [2021)](#about-the-authors). Accordingly, it is expected that all stakeholders in the field of education will develop awareness regarding AI technologies and support their meaningful integration (Kong et al., 2022). The processes through which individuals in education adopt and use AI technologies have become a prominent topic of research across diverse educational contexts (L. Chen et al., 2020). Although this digital transformation is widely

CONTACT Mustafa Erol merol@yildiz.edu.tr Department of Primary Education Program, Yıldız Technical University, \_Istanbul, T€urkiye implemented in primary, middle, and secondary education on a global scale (Ng et al., 2021b), discussions have also emerged in the context of early childhood education, where a gradual process of transformation is currently underway (Su & Yang, 2022; Tao & Nasri, 2025).

The use of AI technologies is increasingly shaping how individuals, particularly educators, interact with children (K. Zhang & Aslan, [2021)](#about-the-authors). The development of these technologies has led to an expan- sion in their applications within the field of education (L. Chen et al., 2020), enabling personalized learning experiences, dynamic assessment processes, and enriched interactive opportunities within online, mobile, and hybrid learning environments (Ng et al., 2021b; S. Wang et al., 2024). The growing availability of these opportunities has sparked greater interest in AI in education (Tapalova & Zhiyenbayeva, 2022). Globally, research on AI in education is gaining momentum, and educational pro- grams are continuously updated in response to technological advancements to ensure the provision of high-quality, future-oriented instruction (D. Chen et al., 2024).

Within this transformation, the exploration of AI self-efficacy, AI anxiety, AI literacy, AI-related atti- tudes, and technology adoption tendencies of teachers and preservice teachers—who are the central actors in instructional processes—is critical for ensuring the quality of integration efforts (D. Chen et al., 2024; Konecki et al., 2024; Morales-Garcıa et al., 2025; Naiseh et al., 2025; Perla et al., 2025; Shao et al., 2025; Syed et al., 2025). AI self-efficacy encompasses individuals’ confidence in using AI technol- ogies, their technical competencies, their comfort in interacting with AI, and their perceived ability to benefit from AI support (Y. Y. Wang & Chuang, 2024). Teachers with high levels of AI self-efficacy tend to use AI-based tools more competently and confidently, which, in turn, contributes positively to teaching and learning processes (Bergdahl & Sjoberg,€ 2025; Mah & Groß, 2024).

AI anxiety has emerged as a critical affective factor that influences how individuals perceive AI, the extent to which they are willing to use it, and the circumstances under which they may resist it (Johnson & Verdicchio, 2017; Schiavo et al., 2024). AI literacy, on the other hand, is a multidimen- sional competency that enables individuals to understand, use, critique, and evaluate AI technologies ethically (Ng et al., 2024; Pinski & Benlian, 2024; Walter, 2024). Achieving effective and sustainable AI integration in education requires that educators acquire AI literacy (Cetindamar et al., 2024; Zhao et al., [2022)](#about-the-authors). Furthermore, both cognitive factors (such as self-efficacy, literacy, and perceived ease of use) and affective tendencies (such as anxiety and attitudes) should be comprehensively evaluated and integrated (Shahzad et al., 2025; L. Wang & Li, 2024).

In today’s rapidly digitalizing world, the widespread adoption of technology brings not only numerous benefits but also growing concerns about its uncontrolled and excessive use. Digital addictions have increasingly been recognized as critical societal and psychological issues (Montag et al., 2025). Initially labeled as “computer addiction” or “internet addiction,” these challenges have been reconceptualized under the term “AI addiction,” while still encompassing similar psychosocial risks (Van Velthoven et al., 2018). In particular, the personalized, persistent, and interaction-based nature of generative AI applica- tions fosters deep emotional and cognitive engagement, which may elevate individuals’ risk of developing addictive tendencies (Huang & Huang, 2025; T. Zhou & Zhang, [2024)](#about-the-authors). Emerging research has highlighted that individuals’ psychological variables—such as their perceptions of AI, levels of AI anxiety, self-efficacy beliefs, and AI literacy—significantly influence their behavioral intentions and usage patterns regarding AI technologies (Alshammari & Babu, 2025;Kuper€ & Kr€amer, 2024; Schepman & Rodway, 2023). Collectively, these findings suggest that the relationship between individuals and technology extends beyond technical interaction to encompass psychological, social, and pedagogical dimensions.

Although literature has made notable progress in this area, the causal relationships between key con- structs—such as AI self-efficacy, anxiety, attitudes, and addiction—remain insufficiently understood. Consequently, the development of structural models capable of elucidating these interactions is impera- tive to provide both theoretical depth and practical guidance. In this regard, the present study aims to investigate the attitudes of early childhood educators (ECEs) and candidates (ECE-C) toward AI, their levels of AI anxiety, self-efficacy, AI literacy, behavioral intention, perceived ease of use, and perceived usefulness to uncover the determinants of their AI addiction tendencies. By proposing a comprehensive model that evaluates individuals’ relationships with AI from a multidimensional perspective, this study aims to illuminate both the opportunities and risks of integrating technology into education.

## 2. Literature review

### 2.1. AI addiction

Research on internet addiction, grounded in the behavioral addiction literature, gained more systematic attention following the inclusion of diagnostic criteria for addiction in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5) by the American Psychiatric Association (2023). Since then, addic- tion tendencies have been investigated in various technological contexts, such as digital addiction, social media addiction, internet addiction, problematic internet use, and technology addiction. Although there is no absolute consensus within the academic community on the definition of addiction, the term is com- monly used to describe behavioral patterns characterized by problematic and withdrawal-related behav- iors that impair individuals’ functioning (Chamberlain et al., 2016; Sussman & Sussman, 2011).

Today, digital technologies offer several social benefits, including enhancing mental well-being (Thapa & Adhikari, 2024), reducing workload, increasing motivation and productivity (C. Zhou, [2023)](#about-the-authors), supporting personalized learning, self-expression, and friendship building, and reducing loneliness (Xie et al., 2023). Despite these advantages, the excessive and purposeless use of digital tools has led to emerging forms of addiction that are increasingly being regarded as a public health concern (Kooli et al., 2025; T. Zhou & Zhang, [2024)](#about-the-authors). The widespread adoption of generative AI systems—such as ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Gemini etc.—has raised concerns that the use of these new technologies may reach pathological levels (Ciudad-Fernandez et al., 2025; H. Li et al., 2025; Yankouskaya et al., [2025)](#about-the-authors). While generative AI tools offer efficiency, they may also foster cognitive dependency by encouraging users to accept AI-generated outputs without verification, thereby weakening critical thinking skills (Gerlich, 2025). In this context, AI literacy plays a vital role in fostering conscious and critical engage- ment with AI technologies, rather than promoting blind reliance (Fui-Hoon Nah et al., 2023).

Passive forms of digital addiction (eg, excessive social media use or watching videos) are often based on one-way content consumption; addiction to generative AI involves active participation, continuous interaction, and creative production—making it distinct from traditional forms of digital addiction (Griffiths, 1995). The propensity for generative AI addiction is characterized by immersive and partici- patory psychological processes, necessitating its categorization as a distinct form of behavioral addic- tion. In this regard, large-scale epidemiological studies investigating the prevalence, demographic distribution, and risk factors of generative AI addiction are essential—particularly for high-risk groups such as students, remote workers, and creative professionals (Kooli et al., 2025; Mustat,a et al., 2025). Given the increasing presence of AI in educational contexts, identifying the cognitive and affective determinants of AI addiction is critical for developing early intervention strategies. Although the funda- mental objective of technological innovation is to enhance human life, the occurrence of unfavorable outcomes at both the individual and societal levels suggests a systemic problem that warrants immedi- ate attention (Shanmugasundaram & Tamilarasu, 2023).

In educational contexts, AI addiction differs from other forms of digital addiction because it involves not only passive content consumption but also continuous interaction, decision-making, and cognitive dependency on intelligent systems. For early childhood educators, this issue is particularly critical, as their pedagogical practices model digital behavior for young children and influence their early technol- ogy attitudes. Understanding their susceptibility to, or protection from, AI addiction is therefore essen- tial to ensuring the ethical and balanced integration of AI in early education settings.

### 2.2. Perceived usefulness, ease of use, and behavioral intention toward AI

Several factors influence individuals’ readiness to integrate AI into education, including their confidence in using technology and their perceptions of its relevance to teaching practices. Perceived usefulness refers to the degree to which individuals believe that using a given technology will enhance their func- tional performance and outcomes (Davis, 1989). In their study, Guo et al. (2025) defined perceived use- fulness as a critical construct for evaluating how teachers assess the potential of AI technologies to improve their work performance and teaching quality. In educational settings, teachers’ intentions to adopt AI are closely tied to their perceptions of its potential to support lesson planning, enhance stu- dent assessments, and facilitate personalized instruction (Choi et al., 2023). User-friendly technologies tend to be perceived as more beneficial, which, in turn, strengthens users’ behavioral intentions to adopt them (Alshammari & Babu, 2025).

High-level perceived ease of use reduces individuals’ cognitive load and increases their motivation and satisfaction when learning to use new technologies (Gkintoni et al., 2025; Izhar et al., 2025). For educators, ease of use plays a key role in mitigating technical complexity and facilitating the integration of technologies into instructional processes (Guo et al., 2025). In AI applications, intuitive interfaces, guided usage features, and user-centered design elements enhance perceptions of ease of use, thereby accelerating the acceptance process (Elshan et al., 2022; Sundar et al., 2025). Davis’ (1989) Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) posits that perceived usefulness and ease of use are fundamental determinants of behavioral intention. This structure has been empirically supported by Guo et al. (2025), who dem- onstrated that teachers’ willingness to adopt AI technologies was strongly predicted by their perceptions of usefulness and ease of use. Similarly, Ma et al. (2025) found that perceived usefulness positively influenced users’ intentions to adopt AI, underscoring that students increasingly value AI’s functional benefits in achieving their learning goals.

### 2.3. AI literacy

AI literacy is a multidimensional competency that extends beyond the ability to use AI technologies; it encompasses the capacity to understand, evaluate, and critically question these technologies through an ethical lens (Ng et al., 2024; Sidra & Mason, 2025). In an increasingly digital world, individuals’ ability to engage meaningfully with AI systems—both technically and ethically—has transformed AI literacy into a fundamental civic skill (Walter, 2024). From this perspective, AI literacy is essential for under- standing and utilizing AI (Liu, 2025). In the field of literature, AI literacy is typically conceptualized along four core dimensions: awareness, usage, evaluation, and ethics (Ng et al., 2024). These compo- nents not only involve familiarity with AI tools but also emphasize the development of critical con- sciousness regarding their broader societal impacts (Cetindamar et al., 2024; Pinski & Benlian, 2024).

From the perspective of Bandura’s (1997) Social Cognitive Theory, AI literacy is a learning outcome shaped by the dynamic interplay of environmental, cognitive, and behavioral factors. Individuals with high levels of AI literacy are not passive consumers of technology; instead, they act as informed, inquisitive, and directive participants in technological systems (Asio, 2024; Shao et al., 2025). These individuals possess the capacity to make informed decisions by recognizing both the benefits and the ethical risks associated with AI technologies. Moreover, empirical studies have shown that AI literacy is positively associated with individuals’ self-efficacy beliefs about technology use (Fui-Hoon Nah et al., 2023). In this regard, the distinguishing feature of AI literacy lies not only in possessing technical knowledge but also in the ability to apply it through a critical and reflective lens (Ng et al., 2024).

Teachers play a central role in developing AI literacy, not only as transmitters of technology but also as guides who instill ethical, pedagogical, and social awareness (Dennison et al., 2024). It is expected that AI-focused educational initiatives launched in higher education institutions will eventually trickle down to lower levels of schooling through teachers (Lin et al., 2021). However, the success of this pro- cess is contingent on enhancing teachers’ AI literacy. Existing research demonstrates that improving teachers’ competencies in this area directly influences their pedagogical self-efficacy and their levels of AI-related anxiety (Ayanwale et al., 2022; Kong et al., 2022). Cultivating ethical, critical, and conscious use of AI in educational settings requires integrating not only technical knowledge but also social sensi- tivity and ethical responsibility into instructional practices. In doing so, AI literacy empowers individu- als to become not merely users of technology but active participants who shape its direction.

### 2.4. Attitudes toward AI

Attitudes toward AI represent a multidimensional psychological construct encompassing individuals’ emotional, cognitive, and behavioral tendencies regarding AI technologies. These attitudes are typically examined along two primary dimensions: positive and negative. Positive attitudes reflect evaluations of AI’s potential to enhance efficiency, convenience, and innovation. In contrast, negative attitudes are often centered on concerns about ethical violations, privacy issues, job insecurity, and the fear that AI

INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF HUMAN–COMPUTER INTERACTION 5

will replace human judgment (Kaya et al., 2024; Schepman & Rodway, 2020). From the perspective of Social Cognitive Theory (Bandura, 1997), attitudes are shaped not only by cognitive judgments but also through observation, experience, and social reinforcement. Positive attitudes toward AI have been found to increase behavioral intention and acceptance of technology, while negative attitudes may con- tribute to anxiety, uncertainty, and resistance to AI use (Montag et al., 2025; T. Zhou & Zhang, [2024)](#about-the-authors).

Attitudes toward AI play a critical role in shaping individuals’ behaviors regarding the adoption and use of new technologies (T. Zhou & Zhang, [2024)](#about-the-authors). These attitudes are influenced by a wide range of individual and contextual factors, including age, gender, educational level, digital literacy, personality traits, and prior technology experience (Kaya et al., 2024). For instance, individuals with high levels of computer literacy, AI knowledge, and positive experiences with technology are more likely to develop favorable attitudes toward AI. In contrast, low self-efficacy and high anxiety levels are associated with the formation of negative attitudes (Asio, 2025; Asio & Suero, 2024). Moreover, attitudes may vary depending on the domain in which AI is applied. In fields where human judgment is less central, such as logistics, astronomy, or data analysis, positive attitudes tend to be more prevalent. In contrast, more cautious or skeptical views are observed in fields requiring ethical decision-making or emotional intelli- gence, such as medicine and psychology (Jungmann & Witthoft,€ 2020; Schepman & Rodway, 2020).

In human-centered domains, such as education, attitudes toward AI directly influence the integration of these technologies in the classroom (Granic, 2022; Zawacki-Richter et al., [2019)](#about-the-authors). Negative attitudes, when coupled with a lack of trust or perceived pedagogical inadequacy, may hinder the adoption of technological innovations (Zawacki-Richter et al., [2019)](#about-the-authors). This resistance can lead not only to limited use of AI in educational contexts but also to imbalanced and ineffective classroom practices. On the other hand, teacher candidates’ positive attitudes toward AI technologies facilitate their creative, ethical, and pedagogically sound use. In this regard, well-structured professional development programs and positive technological experiences may transform educators’ attitudes, thereby enhancing their confidence and willingness to incorporate AI into classroom practices (Nazaretsky et al., 2022; Perla et al., 2025).

### 2.5. AI self-efficacy

AI self-efficacy refers to individuals’ belief in their ability to use AI technologies effectively, consciously, and pedagogically (D. Chen et al., 2024). This concept represents a contextual adaptation of Bandura’s (1977, 1997) notion of self-efficacy, originally developed within the framework of social cognitive theory. According to this theory, individuals’ perceptions of their capacity to perform a specific task directly shape their motivation to learn, cognitive engagement, and behavioral tendencies (Bandura, 1997; Granziera & Perera, 2019). Individuals with high AI self-efficacy tend to demonstrate greater persistence, creativity, and effectiveness in completing AI-related tasks (Montag et al., 2025; Yang et al., [2024)](#about-the-authors). Their interaction with technology extends beyond mere usage; it is also reflected in their pedagogical decision-making, abil- ity to integrate innovative practices, and active participation in digital transformation processes.

Research suggests that AI self-efficacy is not solely rooted in technical skills; it also draws upon eth- ical awareness, comfort with human-centered interaction, and adaptability in learning contexts (Shao et al., 2025). Moreover, this cognitive competency is influenced by a range of individual and demo- graphic variables, including age, gender, educational level, prior technological experience, and cultural context (Naiseh et al., 2025). In line with the principles of observational learning and social reinforce- ment emphasized in social cognitive theory, pre-service teachers’ self-efficacy beliefs can be nurtured through peer interaction, mentoring, and well-designed professional development programs (Falloon, 2020). Indeed, highly active learning environments in which individuals experience positive success out- comes foster increased confidence in AI use and strengthen their ability to view AI not merely as a technical tool, but also as a pedagogical resource (Poulou et al., 2019; Y. Y. Wang & Chuang, 2024).

AI self-efficacy is considered a critical factor influencing teachers’ and pre-service teachers’ decision- making processes regarding the integration of educational technologies into classroom practice (S¸en & Yildiz-Durak, 2022). Individuals with strong self-efficacy beliefs are more likely to adopt creative approaches in pedagogical design. They are often found to experience lower levels of AI-related anxiety and hold more positive attitudes toward AI (D. Chen et al., 2024). In this sense, self-efficacy reflects not only one’s ability to use technology but also an awareness of its ethical, critical, and pedagogical

dimensions. Furthermore, individuals with high AI self-efficacy are believed to use technology more independently and consciously, making them more resilient to digital addiction (Herzallah & Makaldy, 2025). Therefore, teacher education programs must move beyond technical skill development to adopt a holistic structure that supports AI self-efficacy, fosters social learning, and integrates affective compo- nents into the learning process.

### 2.6. AI anxiety

AI anxiety refers to a multidimensional psychological state characterized by individuals’ perceptions of uncertainty, fear, and threat concerning the development, functioning, and societal impact of AI tech- nologies (Johnson & Verdicchio, 2017; Y. Y. Wang & Wang, 2022). From the perspective of Social Cognitive Theory (Bandura, 1997), this form of anxiety arises from the interplay among individuals’ cognitive appraisals, prior experiences with technology, and environmental conditions. In the literature, AI anxiety is frequently attributed to concerns such as privacy violations, job insecurity, ethical dilem- mas, and the potential loss of human control (J. Li & Huang, 2020). These emotional responses are often intensified in contexts where technological advancement occurs rapidly, and individuals lack the necessary knowledge or experience to adapt effectively (Shin, 2021).

Although AI anxiety varies across individuals, it is influenced by a range of individual and demo- graphic variables, including age, gender, education level, self-efficacy, frequency of computer use, and level of AI-related knowledge (Kaya et al., 2024). In the field of education, a key source of this anxiety stems from perceptions that teachers’ professional roles will transform, that decision-making processes will be automated, and that ethical responsibilities may become uncertain (Hopcan et al., 2024; Luckin et al., 2022). Additionally, the potential of AI systems to generate inaccurate or misleading information has raised concerns among educators that extend beyond pedagogy into domains of safety, responsibil- ity, and ethics (Agca & Korkmaz, [2025;](#ethical-approval) X. Li & Zaki, 2024). This affective tension experienced by edu- cators in response to AI can directly influence their willingness and methods to integrate technology into classroom environments, thereby disrupting the overall process of technological transformation in education (Sanusi et al., 2023).

### 2.7. Theoretical framework

This study investigates individuals’ engagement with AI technologies and their potential susceptibility to AI addiction through the combined lenses of the Uses and Gratifications (U & G) Theory and the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM). The U & G theory posits that individuals utilize media and techno- logical tools not solely for passive content consumption but also to fulfill their social, cognitive, and psy- chological needs through intentional and goal-oriented behavior (Rubin, 2009). Taking a user-centered perspective, this theory explains the motivations behind technology use in terms of user needs, individual differences, and expected gratifications. Building upon this foundation, the Uses–Gratifications–Addiction (UGA) model suggests that technologies initially adopted for functional purposes may gradually evolve into habitual and even pathological usage patterns, ultimately leading to addictive tendencies.

On the other hand, TAM is a widely applied model that explains individuals’ adoption of new technol- ogies. According to this model, users’ behavioral intentions to use technology are shaped by two core per- ceptual constructs: perceived usefulness (the belief that using technology will enhance individual performance) and perceived ease of use (the belief regarding the effort required to learn and use the technology) (Davis, 1989). These constructs not only influence behavioral outcomes but also shape cognitive and affective responses, including self-efficacy beliefs, attitudes, and anxiety. Within this frame- work, it has been argued that TAM-related variables are meaningfully associated with individuals’ self- assessments in technological contexts (Viberg et al., 2025; S. Wang et al., 2024; C. Zhang et al., [2023)](#about-the-authors).

The integration of TAM and U & G provides a complementary framework for understanding both the functional and motivational mechanisms that may lead to AI addiction. According to Davis (1989) and subsequent extensions (Alshammari & Babu, 2025), TAM explains how individuals’ perceptions of useful- ness and ease of use shape their behavioral intentions and sustained engagement with technology. In con- trast, U & G theory (Rubin, 2009) emphasizes the intrinsic motivations—such as curiosity, efficiency,

INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF HUMAN–COMPUTER INTERACTION 7

social connection, and validation—that drive users’ continued interaction with technological tools. When these gratifications are repeatedly reinforced, behavioral intention may evolve from purposeful engage- ment to habitual or even compulsive use (Montag et al., 2025). In this sense, TAM variables reflect the cognitive antecedents of technology engagement, whereas U & G variables capture its affective and motiv- ational drivers. The convergence of these perspectives thus offers a theoretically coherent explanation of how positive evaluations of AI (usefulness, ease of use) and the pursuit of psychological gratification (curi- osity, efficiency, validation) may together foster dependence on AI technologies. This integration aligns with recent empirical models, which highlight that user satisfaction and perceived gratification mediate the transition from acceptance to overuse (Guo et al., 2025; S. Zhang et al., [2024)](#about-the-authors).

By integrating these two theoretical perspectives, the present research model posits that individuals’ tendencies toward AI addiction are not solely determined by frequency of use or exposure but are also influenced by a range of multidimensional psychological and perceptual factors, including self-efficacy, AI anxiety, attitudes, behavioral intention, and AI literacy. The increasing adoption of AI in educational settings further underscores the importance of understanding how these individual tendencies impact pedagogical practices. Accordingly, the study aims to explain AI-related addiction risks from a multidi- mensional perspective by analyzing user motivations and the psychological dynamics underlying human–AI interactions in educational contexts.

### 2.8. Current study

#### 2.8.1. Research hypotheses Perceived usefulness of AI has emerged as a critical determinant of individuals’ self-efficacy in using AI technologies. Individuals who believe AI is beneficial tend to report higher self-efficacy in using such technologies. The literature consistently emphasizes a positive and significant relationship between self- efficacy and perceived usefulness (Ma et al., 2025). Likewise, the perception that AI technologies are easy to use also positively influences individuals’ AI self-efficacy. When users perceive a technology as easy to use, they tend to engage with it more confidently and comfortably, thereby strengthening their self-efficacy beliefs (Osman, 2025). Behavioral intention to use AI also reinforces individuals’ AI-related self-efficacy. Those who demonstrate a strong willingness to adopt AI technologies tend to feel more capable of using them effectively (Hong, 2022). Moreover, individuals with high AI self-efficacy exhibit lower levels of AI addiction (Morales-Garcıa et al., 2025). Based on these findings, the following hypotheses were proposed:

H1: Perceived usefulness of AI positively predicts AI self-efficacy.

H2: Perceived ease of use of AI positively predicts AI self-efficacy.

H3: Behavioral intention toward AI positively predicts AI self-efficacy.

H4: Perceived usefulness indirectly reduces AI addiction through self-efficacy.

H5: Perceived ease of use indirectly reduces AI addiction through self-efficacy.

H6: Behavioral intention indirectly reduces AI addiction through self-efficacy.

AI literacy has been shown to enhance individuals’ self-efficacy beliefs about learning and using AI, while also fostering a more positive outlook regarding the societal value of these technologies (Asio, 2024; Becirovic et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2023). This growing awareness indirectly influences behavioral intention, enabling individuals to exhibit stronger tendencies toward technology adoption (Du et al., 2024). Increased AI literacy not only supports practical usage but also strengthens individuals’ self-effi- cacy in handling AI technologies (Fui-Hoon Nah et al., 2023; Kong et al., 2022). Those with greater understanding and practical skills in AI tend to feel more confident in completing AI-related tasks (Becirovic et al., 2025; Bewersdorff et al., 2025; Du et al., 2024). Prior studies suggest that AI literacy enables individuals to approach AI with a more critical, ethical, and informed perspective, thereby enhancing self-efficacy and mitigating the risk of addiction (Ng et al., 2021b; B. Wang et al., 2023).

A negative relationship has also been identified between AI literacy and AI anxiety. Individuals with higher levels of AI literacy tend to report lower anxiety toward these technologies (Schiavo et al., 2024;

1. Zhang et al., [2025)](#about-the-authors). In classroom settings, this relationship is particularly relevant, as it helps reduce students’ anxiety and encourages more confident self-expression (Q. Zhang et al., [2025)](#about-the-authors). Furthermore, a weak but negative association has been observed between AI literacy and negative attitudes toward AI (Bewersdorff et al., 2025). Individuals with high levels of AI knowledge experience lower levels of anx- iety and demonstrate stronger beliefs in their ability to use AI effectively. Accordingly, the following hypotheses were proposed:

H7: AI literacy positively predicts AI self-efficacy.

H8: AI literacy negatively predicts AI anxiety.

H9: AI literacy indirectly reduces AI addiction through self-efficacy.

H10: AI literacy indirectly increases AI addiction through anxiety and self-efficacy.

Negative attitudes toward AI shape not only how often individuals use AI technologies but also their emotional responses to them. Schepman and Rodway (2020) emphasize that positive attitudes toward AI are associated with emotions such as well-being, happiness, and excitement, whereas negative atti- tudes are rooted in uncertainty, fear, and anxiety. Positive attitudes may foster a healthier and more functional engagement with AI, while negative attitudes may heighten anxiety and promote addiction tendencies (Albino et al., [2025;](#ethical-approval) Montag et al., 2025; Schepman & Rodway, 2020). Teachers need to develop the competence to use AI technologies confidently and effectively in both teaching and learning contexts (Falloon, 2020). Some studies have explored the relationship between technology-related anx- iety and AI usage. AI may help alleviate technology anxiety, while technology anxiety may hinder users’ ability to make intelligent decisions. The following hypotheses were formulated:

H11: AI anxiety negatively predicts AI self-efficacy.

H12: AI anxiety indirectly increases AI addiction through self-efficacy.

H13: Negative attitudes toward AI positively predict AI anxiety.

H14: Negative attitudes toward AI positively predict AI addiction.

H15: Positive attitudes toward AI negatively predict AI addiction.

H16: Negative attitudes indirectly increase AI addiction through anxiety and self-efficacy.

It has also been reported that individuals who feel confident in using AI technologies tend to engage with them more frequently and intensively, which in turn may increase their risk of addiction (Morales- Garcıa et al., 2025; S. Zhang et al., [2024)](#about-the-authors). This finding suggests that self-efficacy may not serve solely as a protective factor but could also operate as a risk-enhancing mechanism under certain conditions. Similarly, individuals with higher levels of AI anxiety have been found to exhibit greater addiction tenden- cies (Morales-Garcıa et al., 2025). These findings imply that AI anxiety is not merely a transient or super- ficial emotional response but a structural determinant that influences technology-use and adoption behaviors (Shin, 2021). Individuals with high AI anxiety are more likely to develop negative attitudes, avoid technology use, or engage with it in a limited capacity (Ran et al., 2022; Y. Y. Wang & Wang, 2022). Based on these insights, the following hypotheses were added:

H17: AI self-efficacy negatively predicts AI addiction.

H18: AI anxiety positively predicts AI addiction.

#### 2.8.2. Research questions The rapid and widespread integration of AI technologies into educational environments necessitates a closer examination of teachers’ and preservice teachers’ dispositions toward these technologies (Ng et al., 2023; S. Wang et al., 2024). Technical competencies do not solely determine engagement with AI, but also by individuals’ self-efficacy beliefs, attitudes, levels of anxiety, and literacy skills (Schiavo et al.,

INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF HUMAN–COMPUTER INTERACTION 9

2024; Viberg et al., 2025). Educators’ ability to use AI effectively, ethically, and pedagogically plays a critical role in ensuring the functional and sustainable integration of these technologies in educational contexts (Falloon, 2020; Kong et al., 2022). Furthermore, individuals’ positive or negative attitudes toward AI (Schepman & Rodway, 2020), along with their anxiety levels, may directly influence their usage experiences and shape the sustainability of their engagement with AI—potentially increasing the risk of pathological addiction (Montag et al., 2025).

AI addiction appears to be linked not only to frequency of use or technical ability but also to indi- viduals’ subjective perceptions, emotional responses, and cognitive capabilities (Alshammari & Babu, 2025). For example, high levels of AI literacy are associated with increased self-efficacy, which, in turn, serves as a protective factor against addiction (Becirovic et al., 2025; Du et al., 2024). Conversely, nega- tive attitudes and high levels of anxiety weaken individuals’ relationships with AI technologies and ele- vate the risk of addiction (Schepman & Rodway, 2020; Q. Zhang et al., [2025)](#about-the-authors). Therefore, understanding individuals’ engagement with AI requires the development of multidimensional models that consider constructs such as perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, behavioral intention, AI literacy, atti- tudes, self-efficacy, and anxiety (Davis, 1989; Rubin, 2009).

Examining the interrelationships among these variables—specifically in the context of ECE-C—will help clarify the extent to which this group is at risk or possesses protective characteristics within the broader digital transformation process (Ng et al., 2021b; Tao & Nasri, 2025). Accordingly, this study aims to investigate the direct and indirect effects of ECE-C’s AI self-efficacy, anxiety, positive and nega- tive attitudes, perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness, behavioral intention, and AI literacy on AI addiction. The conceptual model is shown in Figure 1. The study seeks to answer the following research questions:

RQ1. What are the relationships among AI literacy, perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, behavioral intention, self-efficacy, anxiety, attitudes, and AI addiction?

RQ2. What are the direct and indirect relationships between perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, behavioral intention, AI literacy, AI self-efficacy, AI anxiety, attitudes toward AI (positive and negative), and AI addiction?

RQ3. Does AI self-efficacy play a mediating role in the relationships between perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, behavioral intention, AI literacy, AI anxiety, and AI addiction? RQ4. Does AI anxiety have a direct effect on AI addiction? Furthermore, does AI anxiety indirectly affect AI addiction through self-efficacy?

RQ5. Does AI literacy influence AI addiction indirectly through anxiety and self-efficacy? RQ6. Do positive and negative attitudes toward AI influence AI addiction directly and/or indirectly through AI anxiety and self-efficacy?

## 3. Method

### 3.1. Research design

This study employed a quantitative, correlational, cross-sectional research design, utilizing structural equation modeling (SEM) to examine the direct and indirect relationships among self-efficacy, literacy, perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, anxiety, and attitude factors predicting AI addiction among early childhood educators and candidates. This design was selected to test the hypothesized structural model and evaluate the fit of the proposed relationships at a single time point. SEM was particularly appropriate because it enables the simultaneous examination of multiple direct and mediated (indirect) relationships and provides goodness-of-fit indices to assess the adequacy of the overall model.

### 3.2. Participants

The study sample consisted of 509 early childhood educators and candidates—a term used in this study to collectively refer to preservice teachers (students enrolled in early childhood or elementary education programs) and in-service teachers currently working in these fields. The sample was selected through convenience sampling, a method commonly preferred in behavioral and educational research when par- ticipants are readily accessible and relevant to the study’s scope (Etikan et al., 2016). Among the partici- pants, 85.3% were female (n ¼ 435) and 14.7% were male (n ¼ 74). Participants were affiliated with early childhood–related fields, including preschool education (26.2%), primary education (21.8%), and child development (17.6%). Additionally, 22.4% (n ¼ 114) were employed as preschool or elementary school teachers, with an average of 16 years of professional experience. Among undergraduate students, the distribution by academic year was as follows: 36.1% were first-year students (n ¼ 184), 30.0% were second-year students (n ¼ 152), 21.4% were third-year students (n ¼ 109), and 12.5% were fourth-year students (n ¼ 66). The sample size of 509 participants was deemed sufficient for SEM. According to Kline (2016), a minimum sample size of 200 is considered adequate for SEM, and Hair, Black, et al. (2019) recommend a 5–10 participants per estimated parameter rule. Thus, the current sample size exceeds the recommended threshold, ensuring adequate statistical power for model estimation. [Table](#3-method) [1](#3-method) presents demographic information about the participants.

### 3.3. Data collection instruments

#### 3.3.1. Teachers’ Acceptance of Artificial Intelligence (TAAI) To measure ECE-C’s acceptance of AI technologies in educational settings, this study utilized the TAAI scale. The original version of the scale was developed by Guo et al. (2025) and was adapted into Turkish by researchers. The scale consists of 27 items grouped under five subscales: perceived useful- ness, perceived ease of use, behavioral intention, self-efficacy, and anxiety. The construct validity of the Turkish version was confirmed through both exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses. Exploratory factor analysis (EFA) supported by parallel analysis yielded a five-factor structure, explaining 68.5% of the total variance. Factor loadings ranged from .46 to .91, with no cross-loadings detected. Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) results also indicated a good model fit (v2/df ¼ 2.07, RMSEA ¼ 0.061, CFI ¼ 0.92, TLI ¼ 0.91, SRMR ¼ 0.060). For convergent validity, item loadings exceeded 0.60 in all subscales, with AVE values above 0.50 and CR values above 0.80. Discriminant validity was sup- ported by inter-factor correlation analyses, which showed low correlations between the anxiety subscale and positively valenced dimensions. Internal consistency reliability was evaluated using Cronbach’s

#### 3.3.2. Dependence on Artificial Intelligence Scale (DAIS) To assess participants’ levels of addiction to AI technologies, the Turkish version of the DAIS devel- oped by Morales-Garcıa et al. (2024) and adapted by Savas¸(2024) was employed. The scale assesses behavioral tendencies such as overreliance on AI, a need for validation, and a compulsion to stay updated on AI developments. It consists of five items rated on a five-point Likert scale (1 ¼ Strongly Disagree, 5 ¼ Strongly Agree), yielding a possible score range of 5–25. Higher scores indicate greater addiction to AI. Psychometric analysis confirmed the scale’s validity and reliability. EFA revealed a uni- dimensional structure, explaining 58.95% of the total variance, with item loadings ranging from 0.541 to 0.617. CFA results indicated a good model fit (v2/df ¼ 2.609; RMSEA ¼ 0.077; SRMR ¼ 0.03; CFI ¼ 0.98; GFI ¼ 0.98; TLI ¼ 0.96). Internal consistency was confirmed with Cronbach’s alpha of 0.82, test–retest reliability of 0.79, CR of 0.879, and AVE of 0.594. A sample item includes: “I feel vulnerable when I do not have access to AI.” In this study, the term “addiction” was utilized instead of “dependence,” consistent with the existing body of related literature. In the present study, additional val- idity and reliability analyses were conducted with the current sample to ensure the appropriateness of the Turkish version of the DAIS. The findings confirmed the single-factor structure obtained in the adaptation study and demonstrated good internal consistency (a ¼ 0.82) and construct validity.

#### 3.3.3. General Attitudes toward Artificial Intelligence Scale (GAAIS) Initially developed by Schepman and Rodway (2020) to assess GAAIS, the scale was adapted into Turkish by Kaya et al. (2024). It comprises two subscales: positive attitudes (12 items) and negative attitudes (8 items), totaling 20 items rated on a five-point Likert scale (1 ¼ Strongly Disagree to 5 ¼ Strongly Agree). After reverse-coding negative items, total scores range from 20 to 100, with higher scores indicating more favorable attitudes toward AI. Internal consistency was high, with Cronbach’s alpha values of a ¼ 0.88 for the Positive subscale and a ¼ 0.83 for the Negative subscale in the original study, and a ¼ 0.89 and a ¼ 0.91, respectively, in the current study. Sample items include: “Artificial Intelligence can provide new economic opportunities for this country” (positive) and “Organizations use Artificial Intelligence unethically” (negative). The Turkish adaptation involved expert translation, bilingual review, and cross-linguistic valid- ation procedures, yielding a structure closely aligned with the original English version.

#### 3.3.4. Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale (AILS) To evaluate participants’ levels of AI-related knowledge, evaluation skills, and ethical awareness, this study employed the AILS, developed by B. Wang et al. (2023). It was adapted into Turkish by C¸elebi et al. (2023). Designed for individuals without specialized AI expertise, the scale comprises 12 items across four subscales: awareness, usage, evaluation, and ethics. Responses are given on a seven-point Likert scale (1 ¼ Strongly Disagree to 7 ¼ Strongly Agree), with three reverse-coded items. CFA results indicated a strong model fit (v2/df ¼ 1.82; RMSEA ¼ 0.04; RMR ¼ 0.03; NFI ¼ 0.95; CFI ¼ 0.98; GFI ¼ 0.96; AGFI ¼ 0.94). Internal consistency, assessed via Cronbach’s alpha, ranged from 0.72 to 0.76 for subscales and was 0.85 for the overall scale. These findings demonstrate the scale’s robust validity and reliability across both its factorial structure and internal consistency. Sample items include: “I can dis- tinguish between smart and non-smart devices” (Awareness) and “After using an AI product or applica- tion for a while, I can evaluate its capacity and limitations” (Evaluation). In the current study, the psychometric properties of the Turkish version of the AILS were reexamined within this specific sam- ple. Confirmatory factor analysis supported the original four-factor structure, and internal consistency coefficients were comparable to those reported in previous studies (a values ranging from 0.73 to 0.86).

### 3.4. Data collection procedure and ethical considerations

Before conducting validity and reliability analyses of the AI Acceptance Scale, the necessary ethical and legal approvals were obtained to initiate data collection. In this regard, ethical approval was obtained from the university’s Ethics Committee. Based on the granted permissions, the research teamcontacted educational institutions across various provinces to reach ECE-C, the study’s target population. The data collection pro- cess lasted approximately two months. During this period, the scale forms were distributed to participants through both online and face-to-face methods. Data were collected from 424 participants via an online sur- vey platform and from 85 participants via in-person administration. All participants were informed in detail about the study’s aim, the voluntary nature of their participation, and the principles of confidentiality. It was clearly stated that all data would be used exclusively for scientific purposes. No data collection was ini- tiated without first obtaining explicit consent from participants and relevant institutional administrators. The instruments were completed individually by the participants outside instructional hours and submitted to the research team in either physical or digital format. None of the data collection tools contained any personally identifiable information, and all data were analyzed in a fully anonymous manner.

### 3.5. Data analysis

All analyses were conducted using Jamovi version 2.6.44. Prior to the main analysis, preliminary procedures were conducted to identify and address missing values and outliers. No missing data or extreme values were detected in the EFA dataset. To examine the construct validity of the measurement tools, both EFA and CFA were conducted. Internal consistency reliability was assessed using McDonald’s omega (x) and Cronbach’s alpha (a) coefficients. Additionally, Pearson’s correlation coefficient was calculated to examine the relationships among variables. Correlation coefficients were interpreted as follows: jrj¼0.10–0.29 (weak), jrj ¼ 0.30–0.49 (moderate), and 0.50 (strong), in line with Cohen’s guidelines (Cohen et al.,2007).

Convergent validity was evaluated using Average Variance Extracted (AVE) and Composite Reliability (CR) values. The assumption of normality was tested by examining skewness and kurtosis values for each subscale. Skewness ranged from −0.87 to 0.68, and kurtosis ranged from −0.24 to 1.03. Since these values fell within the acceptable range of −1 to þ1, univariate normality was assumed (Hair, Risher, et al., 2019). To assess multivariate normality in the CFA dataset, Mardia’s skewness and kurtosis statistics were used, and the results (v2 ¼ 647; p \< 0.001) indicated that the assumption of multivariate normality was met. Accordingly, path analysis was conducted using the Maximum Likelihood (ML) estimation method (Rosseel, 2019).

To evaluate model fit, several indices were used. First, the chi-square-to-degrees-of-freedom ratio (v2/df) was examined. A ratio below five indicates acceptable model fit (Anderson & Gerbing, 1988). However, due to its sensitivity to sample size, this statistic was not interpreted in isolation. The Comparative Fit Index (CFI) was used to assess the incremental model fit, with values 0.90 consid- ered acceptable and 0.95 excellent (Hu & Bentler, 1999). Similarly, values of 0.90 or higher for the Tucker–Lewis Index (TLI) indicate an acceptable fit, while values of 0.95 or higher reflect an excellent fit (Hu & Bentler, 1999). The Root Mean Square Error of Approximation (RMSEA) was used to assess absolute fit, with values \< 0.08 considered acceptable and \< 0.05 indicating a good fit. Additionally, the Standardized Root Mean Square Residual (SRMR) was examined, with values \< 0.08 reflecting acceptable model fit (Byrne, 2010). For the Normed Fit Index (NFI), values of 0.90 and above were interpreted as indicating good model fit (Bentler & Bonett, 1980; Marsh et al., 2004).

## 4. Findings

### 4.1. Descriptive statistics and correlation analysis

As seen in [Table](#42-measurement-model) [2,](#42-measurement-model) the participants’ mean scores are as follows: AI literacy (42.6 ± 7.61), perceived use- fulness (23.5 ± 5.27), perceived ease of use (18.2 ± 4.98), behavioral intention (20.0 ± 4.79), self-efficacy (23.0 ± 5.50), anxiety (16.7 ± 4.88), AI addiction (12.2 ± 4.88), positive attitudes toward AI (43.1 ± 10.66), and negative attitudes toward AI (21.9 ± 8.03). AI literacy was significantly associated with perceived usefulness (r ¼ 0.48), perceived ease of use (r ¼ 0.69), behavioral intention (r ¼ 0.44), self-efficacy (r ¼ 0.65), anxiety (r ¼ 0.15), and positive attitudes toward AI (r ¼ .46). Perceived usefulness showed strong correlations with perceived ease of use (r ¼ 0.61), behavioral intention (r ¼ 0.70), self-efficacy (r ¼ 0.61), AI addiction (r ¼ 0.25), and positive attitudes toward AI (r ¼ 0.63). Perceived ease of use was positively related to behavioral intention (r ¼ .51), self-efficacy (r ¼ 0.74), anxiety (r ¼ 0.21), AI

### 4.2. Measurement model

To evaluate the psychometric properties (validity and reliability) of the constructs used in the study, McDonald’s Omega (x), Cronbach’s Alpha (a), Composite Reliability (CR), and Average Variance Extracted (AVE) values were examined. The internal consistency coefficients and CR values for all scales exceeded the recommended threshold of 0.80. Furthermore, the AVE values for each construct were above the accepted cutoff of 0.50, indicating adequate convergent validity. Discriminant validity was assessed using Fornell and Larcker (1981) criteria, which were met for all constructs. Fit indices of the measurement models indicated that all scales exhibited acceptable to good model fit. Specifically, the measurement model of the Teachers’ Acceptance of AI Scale, which includes the subdimensions of perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, behavioral intention, self-efficacy, and anxiety, demonstrated acceptable fit to the data (v2/df ¼ 1.96, RMSEA ¼ 0.062 \[0.058, 0.066\], SRMR ¼ 0.051, CFI ¼ 0.92, TLI ¼ 0.91). Similarly, the measurement model for the AI addiction Scale showed good model fit (v2/ df ¼ 4.32, RMSEA ¼ 0.081 \[0.052, 0.112\], SRMR ¼ 0.025, CFI ¼ 0.98, TLI ¼ 0.95). The two-factor structure of the General Attitudes toward AI Scale (positive and negative attitudes) also exhibited acceptable fit (v2/df ¼ 2.55, RMSEA ¼ 0.071 \[0.065, 0.076\], SRMR ¼ 0.074, CFI ¼ 0.92, TLI ¼ 0.90). Additionally, the four-dimensional structure of the AI Literacy Scale yielded acceptable fit indices (v2/ df ¼ 2.29, RMSEA ¼ 0.067 \[0.057, 0.078\], SRMR ¼ 0.057, CFI ¼ 0.95, TLI ¼ 0.92).

### 4.3. Path analysis

The results of the path analysis indicated that the proposed model demonstrated good fit to the data. The chi-square test was statistically significant (v2 ¼ 44.2, df ¼ 10, p \< 0.001), and the Satorra–Bentler scaled chi-square value was 40.3 (df ¼ 10, p \< .001). Additional fit indices were as follows: CFI ¼ 0.96, TLI ¼ 0.92, RMSEA ¼ 0.082 (95% CI \[0.058, 0.107\]), and SRMR ¼ 0.023. These values collectively indicate that the model fits the data well. According to the path analysis results, the model explained 33.7% of the variance in AI addiction (95% CI \[0.270, 0.404\]), 23.3% of the variance in AI anxiety (95% CI \[0.170, 0.299\]), and 65.4% of the variance in AI self-efficacy (95% CI \[0.603, 0.700\]). The standardized regression coefficients from the path analysis are presented in Table 3.

The most powerful predictor of AI addiction was positive attitudes toward AI (b ¼ 0.504, p \< 0.001). Negative attitudes toward AI also positively predicted AI addiction (b ¼ 0.259, p \< 0.001). Anxiety was a significant positive predictor of AI addiction (b ¼ 0.138, p \< 0.001), whereas self-efficacy negatively predicted AI addiction (b ¼ −0.170, p \< 0.001). Regarding predictors of AI anxiety, both negative atti- tudes toward AI (b ¼ 0.457, p \< 0.001) and AI literacy (b ¼ 0.151, p \< 0.001) emerged as significant positive predictors. The strongest predictor of self-efficacy was perceived ease of use (b ¼ 0.396, p \< 0.001), followed by behavioral intention (b ¼ 0.265, p \< 0.001), AI literacy (b ¼ 0.204, p \< 0.001), anxiety (b ¼ 0.096, p \< 0.001), and perceived usefulness (b ¼ 0.080, p ¼ 0.044), respectively. Significant indirect effects identified in the path analysis are presented in Table 4.

Among the indirect paths examined, the most substantial indirect effect on AI addiction was observed for perceived ease of use, mediated by self-efficacy (b ¼ −0.067, p \< 0.001). This negative effect suggests that increased perceived ease of use reduces AI addiction by enhancing individuals’ self- efficacy. A significant indirect effect was also found for negative attitudes toward AI-on-AI addiction through anxiety (b ¼ 0.063, p ¼ 0.001), indicating that negative attitudes increase anxiety, which in turn exacerbates AI addiction. A negative indirect effect was identified for the path from AI literacy ! self- efficacy ! AI addiction (b ¼ −0.035, p \< 0.001), showing that AI literacy reduces addiction via increased self-efficacy. Similarly, behavioral intention ! self-efficacy ! AI addiction yielded a signifi- cant negative effect (b ¼ −0.045, p \< 0.001), suggesting that greater behavioral intention reduces addic- tion through enhanced self-efficacy.

When exploring alternative indirect pathways of AI literacy, a positive indirect effect was found for the path AI literacy ! anxiety ! AI addiction (b ¼ 0.021, p \< 0.05), suggesting that AI literacy may unintentionally increase anxiety, which subsequently contributes to AI addiction. However, a small yet significant negative indirect effect emerged for the serial pathway AI literacy ! anxiety ! self-efficacy ! AI addiction (b ¼ −0.002, p \< 0.05), indicating that the increase in anxiety partially undermines the protective role of AI literacy on self-efficacy. Similarly, the serial pathway negative attitudes ! anxiety ! self-efficacy ! AI addiction showed a weak but statistically significant negative effect (b ¼ −0.007, p \< 0.01). The indirect effect of anxiety ! self-efficacy ! AI addiction was small but significant (b ¼ −0.016, p \< 0.01). In contrast, the indirect effect of perceived usefulness on AI addiction through self- efficacy was found to be statistically nonsignificant (b ¼ −0.014, p ¼ 0.074). 5. Discussion

This study aimed to identify the determinants of AI addiction among ECE-C. The findings largely con- firm theoretical expectations and previous research, offering a comprehensive picture of how individu- als’ attitudes toward AI technologies, anxiety levels, perceptions of self-efficacy, literacy levels, and tendencies toward AI addiction are interrelated. This section discusses the significant associations among the key variables, considering relevant literature.

INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF HUMAN–COMPUTER INTERACTION 15

Figure 2. Path analysis model for bilinguals’ creativity p \< 0.001, p \< 0.001, p \< 0.001.

### 5.1. Relationships among variables

The findings of this study revealed strong, significant associations among AI literacy, perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, behavioral intention, and self-efficacy. This result suggests that individuals with higher levels of knowledge, awareness, and ethical sensitivity toward AI technologies are more likely to perceive these tools as functional, accessible, and safe. This interpretation aligns with the perspectives of Ng et al. (2023) who conceptualize AI literacy not only as technical competence but also as the ability to engage with AI critically and consciously. The strong associations of AI literacy with both behavioral intention and self-efficacy further indicate that cognitive competencies regarding technology also shape individuals’ behavioral inclinations (Asio, 2024; Fui-Hoon Nah et al., 2023;Kong et al.,2022). These find- ings support Bandura’s (1997) social cognitive theory, which posits that one’s cognitive and environmental context influences self-beliefs and behavioral tendencies.

Likewise, the strong correlations between the TAM variables—perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use—and behavioral intention and self-efficacy (eg, ease of use and self-efficacy; usefulness and behavioral intention) confirm the relationships proposed by Davis’ (1989) TAM. Consistent with these results, Osman (2025) found that self-efficacy and perceived usefulness were significant predictors of students’ intentions to use AI. Syed et al. (2025) further reported that AI anxiety, AI self-efficacy, and perceived enjoyment significantly influenced perceived ease of use. Similarly, Alwi and Khan (2025) highlighted the importance of all three factors—self-efficacy, perceived usefulness, and ease of use—for the adoption of technology in remote education and the integration of AI tools into learning processes. Gyesi et al. (2025) also emphasized that within the extended TAM framework, perceived usefulness, ease of use, and self-efficacy significantly influenced behavioral intentions to use AI.

Research by Guo et al. (2025) and Choi et al. (2023) similarly demonstrated that perceived function- ality and ease of use played a central role in shaping teachers’ intentions to integrate AI into their instructional practices. These findings suggest that policies and practices aimed at promoting the inte- gration of educational technology should focus on transforming teachers’ perceptions (Hussain et al., 2025; Liao, 2025). Interestingly, perceived ease of use was not only related to self-efficacy but also sig- nificantly associated with both anxiety and AI addiction. This suggests that while perceptions of ease may support engagement, they may also present potential risks. For instance, Gkintoni et al. (2025) noted that user-friendly interfaces reduce cognitive load and improve the user experience. However, studies by Montag et al. (2025) and Huang and Huang (2025) warned that such accessibility may inad- vertently promote excessive or uncontrolled usage. The strong correlation between AI anxiety and negative attitudes suggests that both constructs may stem from affect-laden cognitive distortions. Florin Stanescu and Constantin Romas,canu (2024) reported significant negative correlations between AI anx- iety and positive attitudes toward AI, indicating that individuals with elevated anxiety tend to adopt

more skeptical views of AI technologies. Similarly, Y. Y. Wang and Wang (2022) and Schiavo et al. (2024) emphasized that concerns about ethics, privacy, or job security can lead individuals to perceive AI as threatening, thereby heightening anxiety.

Conversely, the weak correlation between self-efficacy and negative attitudes may suggest that feeling competent is insufficient to override emotionally or culturally driven skepticism. This highlights the limi- tations of cognitive interventions in addressing affective or value-based resistance, underscoring the need for alternative strategies (Schepman & Rodway, 2020). Furthermore, the lack of significant associations between negative attitudes and AI literacy, perceived usefulness, and behavioral intention suggests that such attitudes are less likely to be shaped by rational evaluations and more by emotional or cultural fac- tors. This finding underscores the complexity of individuals’ resistance to technology, which may be rooted in prior experiences, social norms, and ethical concerns (Walter, 2024; T. Zhou & Zhang, [2024)](#about-the-authors).

Consistent with previous studies (Morales-Garcıa et al., 2025; Shin, 2021), this research highlights the multidimensional nature of AI addiction. The current study revealed that AI addiction was signifi- cantly and positively associated with AI anxiety, negative attitudes, and, surprisingly, also with positive attitudes. This finding suggests that both favorable and unfavorable emotional dispositions toward AI may contribute to excessive engagement. Notably, while high self-efficacy is often regarded as a protect- ive factor, its positive association with AI addiction suggests a more complex relationship—one in which confidence in technology use may inadvertently lead to habitual or compulsive usage patterns (Morales-Garcıa et al., 2025; S. Zhang et al., [2024)](#about-the-authors). Although perceived usefulness and ease of use were weak but significant predictors of AI addiction, they appeared to play a secondary role compared to affective variables. The non-significant correlation between AI literacy and addiction further supports the notion that mere cognitive familiarity does not necessarily reduce excessive reliance on AI tools.

### 5.2. Direct and indirect effects on AI addiction

The finding that self-efficacy has a significant and negative effect on AI addiction suggests that individ- uals’ belief in their capacity to use technology effectively acts as a limiting factor against compulsive use. This aligns with Bandura’s (1997) social cognitive theory, which emphasizes the regulatory role of self-efficacy beliefs on behavioral tendencies. Similarly, Huang and Huang (2025) highlight that individ- uals’ self-regulation and efficacy perceptions underlie their ability to interact healthily with digital sys- tems. Supporting this, Estrada-Araoz et al. (2025) reported that increased academic self-efficacy is associated with lower levels of AI addiction. Conversely, the finding that higher anxiety levels increase the risk of AI addiction may indicate a tendency among individuals to use technology as a coping or avoidance mechanism—suggesting that their engagement with AI is not always grounded in healthy emotional responses. The positive relationship between negative attitudes toward AI and AI addiction may reflect a paradox in which individuals who perceive AI as a source of stress or loss of control still engage with it more intensely. De Freitas et al. (2023) explain this contradiction by noting that, despite distrust and perceived threats, individuals may develop psychological addiction to AI technologies.

On the other hand, positive attitudes toward AI demonstrated a strong protective effect, being the strongest negative predictor of AI addiction in the model. This highlights the role of attitudinal align- ment in regulating technology use and reinforces the importance of cognitive consistency in digital interactions. The finding suggests that cultivating positive attitudes toward AI may reduce tendencies toward addiction and foster healthier digital behaviors (Arslan et al., 2025). Moreover, attitudes toward AI’s potential benefits were positively predicted by subjective knowledge about AI and computer use and negatively predicted by AI-related learning anxiety. Similarly, forgiving attitudes toward AI’s poten- tial disadvantages were positively associated with compatibility but negatively associated with learning and configuration anxiety (Kaya et al., 2024).

Another notable finding is the positive correlation between AI literacy and anxiety. Although this may seem paradoxical at first, it is plausible that individuals with greater knowledge of AI are also more aware of its potential risks and ethical uncertainties. Hence, increased knowledge may not only promote awareness but also elevate emotional burden. At the indirect level, self-efficacy emerged as a central mediator in the model. Notably, the reduction of self-efficacy due to anxiety and its subsequent role in increasing addiction highlights the protective capacity of self-efficacy. The path “negative

INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF HUMAN–COMPUTER INTERACTION 17

attitude ! anxiety ! self-efficacy ! addiction” offers insight into how affective disruptions reinforce addiction. Morales-Garcıa et al. (2025) observed that AI self-efficacy was positively correlated with both AI anxiety and AI addiction. As Ferris et al. (2021) emphasize, modeling the micro-level psychological processes underlying technology addiction necessitates an understanding of such multivariate pathways.

AI literacy appears to reduce AI addiction indirectly by enhancing self-efficacy and reducing anxiety. This implies that technology literacy contributes not only to cognitive competence but also to emo- tional resilience. Guo et al. (2025) similarly argued that digital awareness enables individuals to interact with technology more consciously and self-regulation. Likewise, perceived ease of use was found to reduce addiction indirectly by boosting self-efficacy, suggesting that user-friendly design can support more functional and healthy engagement with technology. This supports Davis’ (1989) TAM model by showing that ease of use is significant not only for intention but also for emotional equilibrium.

Among the five most frequently cited adverse consequences of AI addiction are increased laziness, misinformation, reduced creativity, and diminished critical and independent thinking (S. Zhang et al., [2024)](#about-the-authors). Within this context, the finding that behavioral intention strengthens self-efficacy—and thereby reduces addiction—indicates that positive orientations toward technology may enhance individuals’ sense of control and competence, leading them away from maladaptive behaviors. In summary, key protective factors against AI addiction include self-efficacy, positive attitudes toward AI, perceived ease of use, AI literacy, and behavioral intention. In contrast, the primary risk factors appear to be anxiety, negative attitudes, and the emotional burden they carry. These findings collectively suggest that individ- uals’ relationships with technology are not solely shaped by knowledge. However, any intervention aimed at supporting responsible technology use must also consider emotions, attitudes, and percep- tions, thereby adopting a holistic framework that addresses both cognitive and affective dimensions.

### 5.3. Limitations and future directions

This study provides valuable insights into the psychological and perceptual factors that influence the tendency toward AI addiction among ECE-C, who are key users of AI technologies in the education field. However, the findings should be interpreted in light of several limitations.

The research employed a cross-sectional design, and data were collected at a single point in time. This design limits the ability to draw causal inferences, allowing only correlational interpretations between the variables. To gain a more comprehensive understanding of how positive attitudes toward AI, self-efficacy levels, and AI literacy evolve and influence AI addiction, longitudinal studies are war- ranted. Future research should use longitudinal models to track dynamic variables, such as the duration and frequency of AI exposure. The sample was limited to ECE-C in Turkiye.€ Testing similar models in diverse cultural and educational contexts would be crucial for enhancing the generalizability of the findings. In addition, comparing teachers across different age groups or subject domains may offer interdisciplinary insights into how educators’ experiences and tendencies toward AI addiction vary across contexts. All measurement tools used in this study relied on self-report, which may be subject to social desirability bias. Future research should integrate objective behavioral measures (eg, screen time analytics and frequency logs) and qualitative methods (eg, reflective journaling and in-depth interviews) to offer a more nuanced understanding of individuals’ digital usage patterns.

Despite these limitations, the findings offer several important practical implications. Developing posi- tive attitudes toward AI among teachers and educational technology users should be approached in ways that promote purposeful, conscious technology use rather than reinforcing dependency. Design- centered investments that prioritize user experience and ease of use in AI applications should be emphasized. Moreover, AI literacy training programs must go beyond the transmission of technical knowledge and focus on effective and motivational dimensions. Professional development programs that enhance self-efficacy can serve a protective function by encouraging users to engage with AI tech- nologies more intentionally and in a regulated manner, thereby reducing the risk of AI addiction. Overall, this study contributes to a broader understanding of AI addiction by shedding light on the individual psychological and contextual factors that shape users’ engagement with AI in educational settings.

6. Conclusion

This study revealed that self-efficacy, perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness, AI literacy, AI anxiety, and positive/negative attitudes toward AI play an integrated role in explaining ECE-C’s tendencies toward AI addiction. Notably, positive attitudes toward AI emerged as the strongest predictor of AI addiction, while elevated AI anxiety and lower self-efficacy levels were associated with increased risk of addiction. The structural model demonstrated that individuals’ attitudes and beliefs about AI shape whether they experience this technology as a functional tool, a means of escapism, or a source of loss of control. These findings indicate that approaches focusing solely on the technical aspects of AI inte- gration in education are insufficient. Instead, there is a need for multidimensional professional develop- ment programs that incorporate effective and attitudinal dimensions. It is recommended that teacher education programs prioritize content that enhances AI self-efficacy, reduces anxiety, and fosters informed and constructive attitudes. Moreover, AI literacy should be conceptualized not only as know- ledge but also as the ability to develop ethical, critical, and psychologically balanced relationships with AI technologies. This study contributes to the development of structured models designed to identify and prevent AI addiction. It underscores the importance of promoting a sustainable, balanced, and crit- ical perspective on the use of digital tools in educational contexts.

### About the authors

Merve Canbeldek Erol works as an Assistant Professor in the Department of Preschool Education at Pamukkale University, Denizli, Turk€ ḭye. Her research interests include coding and robotics education, STEM education in early childhood, assessment and evaluation in early childhood, and the quality of preschool educational institutions.

Ahmet Erol is an Associate Professor in the Department of Preschool Education at Pamukkale University, Denizli, Turk€ ḭye. His research interests include environmental education, self-regulation in early childhood, STEM educa- tion in early childhood, and social skills during the preschool period.

Mustafa Erol is an Associate Professor in the Department of Primary Education at Yıldız Technical University, Istanbul, Turk€ ḭye. His research interests include artificial intelligence, early engineering, and STEM education, friendship and collaboration, and migrant education, with a particular focus on primary school children and teacher education.

Kadriye Selin Budak Topaloglu is a lecturer at the School of Health Services, Bilecik S¸eyh Edebali University, and a doctoral candidate in Early Childhood Education at Gazi University. Her research focuses on digital play addiction tendency, parental mediation, technology integration, and spatial thinking in early childhood education and teacher education.
